newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. GDP grew by 4.7 percent in Q4.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. GDP grew by 4.7 percent in Q4.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported gross domestic product (GDP) grew at an annual rate of 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter after an increase of 2.1 percent in the final estimate of the third quarter.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 3.9 percent rise in fourth-quarter GDP.
KEITH EDMONDS, IBJ INTERNATIONL, LONDON: "It was a very stong report; GDP up stongly and also final sales up ... There are clear signs ... that growth is well above trend."
Edmonds was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

ANTHONY KARYDAKIS, SENIOR FINANCIAL ECONOMIST, FIRST CHICAGO CAPITAL MARKETS: "This confirms the impressive momentum the economy had as the year was coming to a close. It shows the second half of the year had almost precisely the same percentage gain as in the first half. We had strength concentrated in two categories as expected, consumption and net exports. I don't think we can draw any inference regarding the pace of growth we'll see in the first quarter."

Karydakis continued: "There was not much change in inventories, which suggests inventories are roughly balanced and there's no reason to expect any significant drawdown or buildup in the first quarter."

KEVIN FLANAGAN, ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "You have a battle going on between the actual growth figure and the inflationary readings. Nevertheless, fourth quarter growth was far more than anybody was looking for, and it is something that's going to keep the (Federal Reserve) on notice that growth is eclipsing their expectations by a visible amount."
Flanagan went on: "The question is: Do you keep this momentum going into 1997? Obviously it is going to be tough to match or top this in the first-quarter."

EVELINA TAINER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, INDOSUEZ CARR FUTURES: "The numbers were boosted by government spending. So while there's certainly indications of a lot of strength in the fourth quarter and we did get good improvement from net exports, there is nothing in this number that would suggest that the first quarter (is) going to be equally strong or even 3.0 percent GDP."

MICHAEL STRAUSS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, SANWA SECURITIES (USA) CO: "We ended the fourth quarter on a strong note, but it doesn't look like there's any added strains on the economy ... It is but another reason for (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan to look at it and say that there is no reason for concern. We had more real growth and less inflation.

"The (Treasury) market should hold in reasonably well because while the GDP print was higher than expected, the components were not that negative. There was a higher inventory level and a little higher consumption spending, and the price (deflator) was less than expected."

TIM O'NEILL, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HARRIS BANK/BANK OF MONTREAL: "Obviously a surprise on the high side. Final sales were obviously very strong. That probably would be the key to it. Plus the export number, which was a very significant bounce. Consumer spending was also a strong rebound.

Commenting on the lower-than-expected chain-weighted price index: "If you look at the other inflation numbers that we've been seeing, that number is consistent. I don't think we've seen yet the full impact of the pressures that are coming on the inflation side from that very tight labor market. Price pressures are not picking up yet.

"We can be reasonably calm about whether the Fed has to tighten, whether the economy is too strong. What we're going to have to see in the first quarter is that the economy is beginning to show some signs of slowing.
"We knew the (GDP) number was going to be strong; the Fed knew it would be strong. This is a story (the central bank) already knew," O'Neill added.
